summary: Describes an interface to the IBM 5250 Telnet server that lets a client request a terminal or printer session with a specific device name. It is an informational memo and was replaced by RFC 4777.

plainLanguage.summary: Old IBM systems want to know which named terminal or printer you are. This describes how a Telnet user can ask for one by name.

questions: how do i select a device name in 5250 telnet
how do i auto sign on to as/400 via telnet
subtitle: Extending Telnet to support IBM terminal device selection and auto sign-on.

tldr.problem: IBM 5250 terminal users need a way to request a specific terminal or printer device by name and automatically sign on with credentials.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends Telnet's environment option negotiation (RFC 1572) to allow clients to specify device names, session attributes, and optionally encrypted passwords during the connection setup.
tldr.outcome: IBM AS/400 systems can now support device-specific terminal sessions and auto-signon, enabling personalized configurations and printer device passthrough. This RFC was superseded by RFC 4777.

today: RFC 2877 is an Informational document that was obsoleted by RFC 4777 in January 2007. It described enhancements to Telnet for IBM 5250 terminal and printer device support with auto-signon capabilities.

sections.title: Telnet Enhancements for Device Selection
sections.content:
RFC 2877 describes extensions to Telnet that allow clients to request specific terminal or printer devices on an IBM AS/400 system, with support for automatic sign-on and password encryption. The enhancements use Telnet's standard environment option negotiations (RFC 1572) to exchange device attributes and credentials.

By allowing clients to specify a device name, applications can request customized terminal configurations for specific users, connect printers directly as Telnet clients, or automate the sign-on process using either clear-text or encrypted passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet now lets you ask for a specific terminal or printer by name when you connect, and optionally log in automatically with your password.

sections.title: Enhanced Option Negotiation
sections.content:
The 5250 Telnet server bundles environment option negotiations alongside standard terminal type negotiations. The client sends USERVAR (user-defined variable) fields to specify device attributes such as device name, keyboard type, code page, and character set.

Key USERVAR parameters include: DEVNAME (device name, up to 10 characters), KBDTYPE (keyboard type like USB), CODEPAGE (character encoding), and CHARSET (character set). The server uses these to either select an existing device or create a new one with the requested attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a list of settings it wants (like the device name and keyboard type) and the server either uses an existing terminal with those settings or creates a new one.

sections.title: Auto-Signon and Password Encryption
sections.content:
The RFC defines custom USERVAR fields for automated authentication. The server sends a random seed value; the client generates its own seed and uses both to encrypt the user's password via a 7-step Data Encryption Standard (DES) scheme compatible with APPC and Client Access. The encrypted password is sent back for authentication.

If encryption is not required, clear-text passwords can be sent in the same USERVAR fields, with an empty or zero seed indicating no encryption. Additional USERVAR fields control the startup environment: IBMRSEED (server random seed), IBMSUBSPW (encrypted password), IBMCURLIB (current library), IBMIMENU (initial menu), and IBMPROGRAM (program to call).
sections.plainLanguage: The server and client swap random numbers and use them to encrypt your password, or you can send the password in plain text if your network is trusted.

sections.title: Printer Device Support
sections.content:
New terminal types have been added for printer devices: IBM-3812-1 (single-byte printer) and IBM-5553-B01 (double-byte printer). Printer-specific USERVAR fields allow clients to configure printers through Telnet, specifying features like message queue names, fonts, form feed types, paper sources, and DBCS language support.

After Telnet negotiation completes, the server sends a Startup Response Record indicating success (codes I901, I902, I906) or failure (codes 2702, 2703, etc.). Pass-through mode allows the client to send and receive print records containing actual print data and status information.
sections.plainLanguage: You can now plug a printer into Telnet and tell it which type of printer it is, what fonts to use, and how to handle paper.

sections.title: Device Collision Handling and Security
sections.content:
When a requested device name is already in use, the server responds with a new SEND request for the DEVNAME USERVAR. The client must propose a different device name. If the same device name is sent twice in a row, the server disconnects the client. This collision handling allows graceful fallback when preferred device names are unavailable.

Clear-text passwords are only secure on physically protected or trusted networks (such as an intranet). If the network is vulnerable to IP address spoofing or is connected to the Internet, encrypted password exchange MUST be used. The password encryption uses the 7-step DES scheme. Passwords longer than 10 characters are not valid; passwords of lengths 9 and 10 require special handling.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone else is already using the terminal you asked for, the server asks you to pick a different one. When sending passwords, encrypt them over untrusted networks.
